claim: Reference Python process-mining library: discovery (Alpha/Heuristics/Inductive miner), conformance checking, XES + OCEL 2.0 event logs, Petri nets/BPMN/process trees.
license_claimed: AGPL-3.0 — dual-licensed; README explicitly offers a separate paid license for commercial use in closed-source environments
activity: 1.0k stars, 355 forks, 9,616 commits on release branch; supports Python 3.9-3.14; maintained by Process Intelligence Solutions (Fraunhofer FIT spin-off)
relevance: The canonical way to turn a client's raw system logs into an observed process model without asking them to describe their process. If Actionist can obtain any timestamped event stream (CRM stage changes, ticket transitions, order states), pm4py yields the as-is workflow, rework loops and bottlenecks as evidence rather than self-report.
limitations: AGPL-3.0 is the trap: linking pm4py into a hosted Actionist service arguably triggers the network-copyleft clause, and the vendor sells a commercial license precisely because of this. Also requires a case ID + activity + timestamp triple that most SMB clients do not have lying around; log extraction is the real work, not the mining.

claim: Open-source Core Edition of the Apromore process-mining platform: log/BPMN importer, portal, Process Discoverer, business calendar, model editor.
license_claimed: LGPL-3.0 (multiple license files present); commercial Apromore Enterprise Edition holds the valuable features
activity: ARCHIVED by owner 29 Aug 2025, read-only; README declares the source deprecated. 143 stars, 79 forks, 12,113 commits
relevance: Useful only as a design reference for what a process-intelligence portal exposes to a non-technical business user — the import/discover/share loop is the UX Actionist would need if it ever surfaced mined processes to a client.
limitations: Dead as a dependency: archived and self-declared deprecated. The open Core deliberately excludes conformance checking, dashboards, filters, simulation, KPIs and root-cause analysis — everything that would make it useful — all reserved for the paid Enterprise Edition. A stars/licence badge reading 'LGPL open source' badly misrepresents what you actually get.

claim: Core R package of the bupaR ecosystem for business process analysis; event-log object model, case/trace statistics, companion packages for discovery and performance analysis.
license_claimed: LICENSE file contains only 'YEAR: 2017 / COPYRIGHT HOLDER: Hasselt University' — the R 'MIT + file LICENSE' stub pattern; MIT is likely but NOT confirmed from the LICENSE body alone
activity: 62 stars, 7 forks, 253 commits, version 1.0.0, lifecycle badge 'stable'; CRAN-published; R-CMD-check CI and codecov active
relevance: The permissive-license escape hatch from pm4py's AGPL problem, if the analysis lane can be R rather than Python. Same evidence value: derive the real process from an event log instead of interviewing the client about it.
limitations: Licence is inferred, not observed — the LICENSE file is a two-line stub and the actual declaration lives in DESCRIPTION, which I did not fetch. Do not quote 'MIT' to Cena without reading DESCRIPTION. R runtime is a poor fit if Actionist's stack is TypeScript/Python. Much smaller ecosystem than pm4py.

claim: R interface bridging bupaR to the Python PM4Py library; exposes inductive miner discovery, Petri net rendering and conformance alignments to R users.
activity: Version-pinned to PM4Py releases (R package 1.1.19 installs PM4Py 1.1.19) per search result; no repo page fetched
relevance: Only interesting as evidence that the two ecosystems interoperate; would let an R-based pipeline reach pm4py's conformance algorithms.
limitations: Not fetched — stars, licence, and activity all unverified. Critically, wrapping PM4Py does not escape PM4Py's AGPL-3.0; the bridge inherits the upstream licensing question rather than solving it.

claim: Curated list of open-source process-mining tools and resources (ProM, Apromore CE, RapidProM, OpenXES).
relevance: Denominator-expansion aid: a map of the ProM/RapidProM/OpenXES corner of the ecosystem that direct search surfaces poorly.
limitations: Awesome-list, not a tool. Curated lists rot; entries are the curator's claims, each needing its own verification. Not fetched.

claim: Collection of process-mining resources.
relevance: Same as oss-b-005 — a pointer into the academic ProM ecosystem.
limitations: Not fetched; list-of-lists with no independent evidence value.

claim: Screen-based task-mining framework for RPA: Django platform capturing UI logs, eye-tracking gaze logs and screenshots, with modules for behaviour monitoring, decision discovery, feature extraction, process discovery and reporting.
activity: 6 stars, 3 forks, 982 commits; University of Seville research project (renamed from 'rim'); Docker deployment with optional NVIDIA GPU images
relevance: Closest academic match to 'watch the work and infer the process' — combines screen capture with decision discovery, which is exactly the precompute-before-ask pattern applied to desktop work.
limitations: DISQUALIFYING for client work: CC BY-NC 4.0 forbids commercial use, and Action Model work is commercial. A licence badge glance would call this 'open source' and be wrong for our purposes. Also a 6-star single-lab research artifact with heavy deps (Graphviz, MS Word/LibreOffice, C++ toolchain). Gaze tracking raises an obvious consent problem.

claim: User-interaction logger for robotic process mining; Excel add-in passive listener plus Chrome extension, writing captured UI events to CSV.
activity: ARCHIVED by owner 29 Aug 2025, read-only. 19 stars, 9 forks, 127 commits, Node.js
relevance: Reference implementation of the narrowest viable capture surface: just Excel and the browser, the two places most SMB knowledge work actually happens. The CSV-per-interaction schema is a useful pattern to copy even though the code is dead.
limitations: Archived, same day as ApromoreCore — the whole Apromore open-source line was retired together. Covers only Excel + Chrome. Capturing keystrokes and cell contents inside a client's spreadsheets is about as invasive as capture gets.

claim: Compiles a demonstrated GUI workflow into a deterministic, locally executable program; captures structural, accessibility, visual, OCR, spatial and transition evidence across browser, Windows, macOS, Linux, RDP and Citrix/VDI.
activity: 1.7k stars, 263 forks, 1,157 commits; actively restructuring from a pre-1.0 monolith (v0.46.0, frozen under legacy/) into a multi-repo split (flow, capture, privacy, desktop)
relevance: The strongest task-mining candidate. Its explicit design claim — zero generative-model calls on healthy runs, halt instead of guess — is the discipline Actionist wants when inferring a client's process from observation: produce an inspectable artifact, refuse to hallucinate the gaps.
limitations: Mid-refactor, so the API surface is unstable and the legacy monolith is frozen rather than maintained; adopting now means tracking a moving multi-repo target. Screen+keyboard+OCR capture on a client machine is the maximum-invasiveness end of the spectrum. The PII/PHI scrubbing lives in a separate optional extra, meaning the safe configuration is opt-in, not default.

claim: NeurIPS 2025 spotlight framework for computer-use agents: AgentNetTool cross-platform recorder, AgentNet dataset of 22.6K human-annotated desktop tasks across 200+ apps, AgentNetBench evaluator, OpenCUA 7B/32B/72B models.
license_claimed: MIT — README explicitly states use permitted for research, educational AND commercial purposes
activity: 826 stars, 108 forks, 75 commits; dated updates through 2026-01-17 (vLLM support); OpenCUA-72B ranked #1 open-source on OSWorld-Verified at 45.0%
relevance: AgentNetTool is the best-licensed demonstration recorder found: synchronized screen video, mouse/keyboard events AND accessibility trees, plus a browser-based review/trim/submit step. That human review gate before submission is the exact consent pattern Actionist should copy — the client sees and edits what gets captured before it leaves the machine.
limitations: The recorder is instrumental to a model-training agenda, not a product; expect research-grade ergonomics and thin support. Accessibility-tree capture pulls in whatever text is on screen, including material the client never meant to share. Dataset claim varies by source (22.5K vs 22.6K) — quote the repo's 22.6K.

claim: Cross-platform automated time tracker; aw-watcher-window logs focused application and window title, aw-watcher-afk infers active/idle from keyboard and mouse, aw-watcher-web browser extension tracks active tab title and URL.
activity: 18.7k stars, 991 forks, 1,130 commits; 169 open issues; Rust server rewrite (aw-server-rust) slated to become the default; decentralized sync still WIP
relevance: The lowest-invasiveness, highest-maturity capture option: app names, window titles and tab URLs are enough to infer which systems a client actually lives in and roughly how their day splits, without recording screen content or keystrokes. This is the pragmatic tier-1 sensor for precomputing client context.
limitations: Gives app-level attention data, not process structure — you learn they spend four hours in HubSpot, not what workflow they run inside it. Window titles leak more than users expect (document names, customer names, subject lines); one adapted fork exists specifically to disable window-title tracking, which is itself evidence that the default is too revealing. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft: modifications to ActivityWatch files must be published, though it will not infect surrounding proprietary code.

claim: macOS record-and-replay workflow recorder for computer-use agents; captures mouse, keyboard and UI events as structured traces (session.json, events.jsonl), validates recording quality and packages evidence for an agent skill-creation flow.
relevance: Its stated thesis — one demonstration should carry enough evidence for an agent to learn the task — is precisely the precompute-before-ask premise. The recording-quality validation step is a pattern worth stealing: refuse a capture that is too thin to be evidence, rather than proceeding and asking later.
limitations: Not fetched: licence, stars, and maintenance all unverified. macOS-only per its own description, which excludes most business clients. Appears very new and likely single-maintainer.

claim: Ui.Vision open-source RPA with computer vision, OCR, Anthropic Computer Use/LLM integration and a web macro recorder; Selenium IDE import/export.
relevance: Execution-side rather than discovery-side, but its macro recorder is a capture surface and its Selenium IDE compatibility shows a path from a recorded demonstration to a portable, inspectable script.
limitations: Not fetched. Ui.Vision historically ships a free core with paid XModules/enterprise tiers, so 'open-source' likely understates the commercial boundary — needs the LICENSE read before any claim. Primarily an automation runner, not a process-discovery tool.

claim: Free RPA tool by AI Singapore covering websites, desktop apps and CLI; cross-platform; flows writable in 22 languages.
relevance: Execution lane only; marginal to evidence-gathering.
limitations: Not fetched. Automation execution, not discovery — it replays what you already know, it does not tell you what the client does.

claim: Collection of open-source RPA libraries for Robot Framework and Python.
relevance: Library-level automation primitives; no discovery capability.
limitations: Not fetched. Execution side; does not extract evidence about a client's process.

claim: Multi-agent enrichment pipeline turning an email/domain into a company profile: industry, business model, employee count, founding year, HQ, funding stage and investors, tech stack, plus custom fields — every field carrying source URLs.
activity: 1.3k stars, 314 forks, only 35 commits on main; Next.js 15
relevance: The single most directly transferable pattern in this survey: given nothing but a client's email address, produce a cited company dossier before the first conversation. The per-field source-URL citation is the design detail that makes precomputed context defensible — Cena can see where each claim came from instead of trusting a model.
limitations: MIT covers the orchestration shell only; the actual capability is rented — it will not run without a Firecrawl API key and an OpenAI key, so both cost and data flow sit with third parties. 35 commits is a demo-scale codebase, essentially a showcase for Firecrawl's paid API (compare the Composio pattern: permissive licence over a paid hosted dependency). Synthesis is GPT-4o-mediated, so field values are model outputs, not scraped facts.

claim: All-in-one website OSINT tool running ~40 checks: DNS, SSL/TLS config and cipher suites, HTTP and security headers, cookies, Whois, robots.txt, sitemap/listed pages, open ports, traceroute, trackers, tech stack via Wappalyzer fingerprints, email config (DMARC/DKIM/SPF/BIMI), WAF detection, Wayback archive history, Tranco global rank, screenshots.
activity: 34.6k stars, 2.8k forks, 691 commits; only 5 open issues against 27 open PRs; hosted demo at web-check.xyz plus Codeberg mirror
relevance: Pure-observation client intelligence from nothing but a domain: which analytics and payment stacks they run, whether email auth is configured, how the site has changed over years of Wayback history, whether they have a WAF. All of it inferable before asking the client a single question, and all from data they publish anyway.
limitations: Reveals infrastructure, not process — it cannot tell you how the client works internally. Full coverage needs nine optional third-party API keys (Shodan, SecurityTrails, BuiltWith, Cloudmersive, Tranco, urlscan and others), each with its own cost and data-sharing implication; README itself warns REACT_APP_-prefixed keys are exposed client-side. Some checks (open ports, traceroute) probe the target's infrastructure — fine on a client who engaged us, questionable on a prospect who did not. The 27-open-PR against 5-open-issue ratio suggests contributions outrunning maintainer review.

claim: Extracts 700+ technologies from a repository — languages, SaaS products, cloud, infrastructure, dependencies and services — by parsing package.json, docker-compose.yml, go.mod and similar manifests, and mapping folder-to-service relationships.
activity: 425 stars, 24 forks, 930 commits; no archive/deprecation notice; semantic-release, Renovate, codecov, changelog, and a documented semver policy for both API and detection rules; powers getstack.dev
relevance: Bridges enrichment and introspection: if a client grants repository access, their manifests confess the actual SaaS and infrastructure they depend on — no survey required. Note that detection-rule semver is exactly the kind of contract that makes a tool safe to depend on for a repeated deliverable.
limitations: Requires the client to hand over source code, a far higher trust bar than a domain lookup, and only works for clients who have a codebase at all — most non-technical SMB clients do not. Sees declared dependencies, not runtime reality: a package.json entry proves nothing is actually used in production. Full support is limited to nine ecosystems, with Java, C#, Terraform and others only partial.

claim: Open-source suite of six lead-enrichment tools intended to be cloned, customized and self-hosted with your own API keys; reference stack Railway + Vercel + Supabase + Resend at roughly $10-20/mo.
relevance: Evidence about the shape of the category rather than a component to adopt: the self-host-the-shell, rent-the-data pattern recurs across every OSS enrichment project found.
limitations: Not fetched — licence, stars and maintenance unverified. By its own framing the tools are thin wrappers requiring your own paid API keys, so the open-source part carries little of the value.

claim: Self-hosted CLI agent for B2B lead generation: describe a product, it finds matching people from a licensed data provider and explains the fit, exporting CSV. Claims zero platform-ToS surface — browserless, no social account, no scraping.
relevance: Interesting mainly for its explicit ToS-surface stance: it markets not-scraping as the feature. If Actionist precomputes client context, the same posture (use licensed or public data, never scrape a platform in breach of its terms) is the defensible line.
limitations: Not fetched. 'Licensed data provider' means the data is bought, not free — the open-source code is again the shell around a paid dependency. Outbound-prospecting oriented rather than client-understanding oriented.

claim: AI-assisted OSINT tool for information gathering and situational analysis.
relevance: Adjacent: collection-and-analysis pipeline architecture for open-source intelligence, applicable in shape to continuous monitoring of a client's public footprint.
limitations: Not fetched. Oriented to security/threat news aggregation rather than company or process intelligence.

claim: Curated list of OSINT tools and resources.
relevance: Denominator-expansion aid for the public-footprint corner of client intelligence.
limitations: Not fetched; curated list, entries are unverified claims, notorious for link rot.

claim: Captures and analyzes API traffic to reconstruct OpenAPI specifications with no code instrumentation, then diffs observed traffic against approved specs to flag Shadow APIs (observed but undocumented) and Zombie APIs (deprecated but still live).
activity: ARCHIVED by owner 29 May 2026, read-only. 576 stars, 74 forks, 272 commits
relevance: The clearest statement of the introspection pattern in the whole survey: infer the true integration surface from observed traffic, then treat the gap between documented and observed as the finding. That gap — what the client's systems actually do versus what anyone documented — is exactly the value Actionist claims to deliver.
limitations: Archived three months ago, so unmaintained and accumulating unpatched CVEs in a security-adjacent tool. Assumes a Kubernetes/service-mesh estate (Istio 1.10+, DaemonSet tap, Kong, Tyk or OTel collector); can run with ENABLE_K8S=false but that is the degraded path. Requires deploying a traffic tap inside the client's production cluster — a very high authority and trust bar, and it observes real request/response payloads including customer data.

claim: Normalizes HTTP traffic from HAR files, Postman collections, Playwright/Puppeteer/Cypress captures, mitmproxy/Charles logs and Go http.Client into a versioned intermediate representation ('ir.v1'), then infers OpenAPI 3.0/3.1/3.2 specs — detecting path/query params, types and formats, auth schemes and pagination patterns, and diffing specs for breaking changes.
activity: 3 stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers, 120 commits, no tagged releases. Strong hygiene despite that: Go CI, lint, CodeQL SAST, MkDocs site, CHANGELOG, ROADMAP, security policy, adapters in Go/Python/TypeScript
relevance: The low-authority alternative to APIClarity: a HAR file exported from the client's own browser DevTools during a normal working session reveals which internal and third-party APIs their tools call, with no agent installed and no cluster access. That is an unusually cheap way to precompute a client's real integration map.
limitations: 3 stars and zero forks — a single-maintainer, pre-release project with essentially no production validation; the engineering hygiene is genuine but is not adoption. HAR captures contain live auth tokens, cookies and response bodies, so the artifact itself is a credential-bearing secret that must be scrubbed before it is stored or shared. Inference from a single session sees only the endpoints that session happened to touch.

claim: Google Sheets add-on for Workspace admins: security-posture checklist plus read-only Admin SDK inventory scripts covering users, license assignments, Groups settings and membership, mobile devices, shared drives, OAuth tokens (getOAuthTokens.gs), app passwords, OUs, domains and DNS.
activity: 29 stars, 6 forks, 133 commits; empty Releases/Contributors sections in the fetched page, so maintenance cadence could not be established
relevance: The most practical SaaS-discovery route found for a normal business client. The OAuth token report answers 'which third-party applications has this organization actually connected to its Google Workspace' — a direct, evidence-based read of the client's real tool stack, obtained without watching anyone work.
limitations: Requires super-admin credentials on the client's Workspace tenant — the highest authority ask in this survey, and it cannot be run against an external organization, so it is strictly a post-engagement tool. Inventories OAuth tokens rather than applications per se. Output sheet contains the full directory (names, emails, group memberships) and is therefore a personal-data artifact from the moment it is generated. Small project, maintenance unverified.

claim: Widely-used community PowerShell script enumerating all delegated and application permission grants in Entra ID, iterating app permissions directly rather than parsing logs; updated to handle tenants with 1000+ grants.
relevance: Microsoft 365 counterpart to the Workspace OAuth inventory: the consented-app list is a direct enumeration of the SaaS a client's staff have actually wired into their identity provider.
limitations: A gist, not a maintained project — no licence, no releases, no issue tracker, no security review. Needs Graph admin consent on the client tenant. Not fetched.

claim: Entra ID governance toolkit to list, audit and bulk-delete Microsoft Graph delegated user consents, forcing least-privilege re-consent; PowerShell 5.1 and 7+, revocation path uses pure REST with no module dependency.
relevance: The listing half is the useful half: enumerate oauth2PermissionGrants to see what each user consented to, giving a per-user view of shadow SaaS adoption inside the client.
limitations: Not fetched. Ships destructive capability (bulk consent deletion) alongside read-only inventory — the wrong tool to hand an automated agent, and a serious blast-radius risk if scoped wrongly on a client tenant. Individual-maintainer project despite the -msft handle; that suffix is not a Microsoft support guarantee.

claim: Playwright-based tool capturing real-time API traffic from web applications and generating structured API intelligence — schema inference, automatic endpoint classification (AUTH, USER), and an OpenAPI generator.
relevance: Same HAR-style pattern as traffic2openapi but driven by Playwright, so the capture can be scripted against a client's web tool rather than depending on a manual DevTools export.
limitations: Not fetched — licence, maturity and maintenance all unknown; named as a reverse-engineering tool, which is a framing worth care in a client context. Driving Playwright against a third-party SaaS the client uses may breach that vendor's terms of service.

claim: Self-hostable product-integration platform providing managed OAuth and unified syncs across a large catalog of third-party SaaS APIs.
license_claimed: NOT OBSERVED — fetch failed; Nango has historically used a mixed model with an Elastic-style restriction on parts of the platform, which must be read from the repo before any claim
activity: not observed — the github.com/nango/nango path 404s; correct path is NangoHQ/nango, which I could not fetch before the rate limit
relevance: If Actionist needs to read a client's live SaaS data (CRM records, ticket histories) to precompute context, a self-hosted integration layer is the alternative to building dozens of OAuth flows. That live data is also the highest-value raw material for process mining — it is where the event logs actually live.
limitations: Nothing verified. The licence in particular is a known trap in this category (compare the Composio finding: a permissive SDK badge over a paid hosted API), and connector counts in this space routinely conflate 'services listed' with 'working OAuth integrations'. Do NOT quote a connector count or a licence for Nango until the repo and LICENSE body have been read directly.

claim: Open-source API security platform whose code-analysis tool scans source repositories to discover APIs including shadow APIs, integrating with traffic-based inventory and CI/CD to catch new APIs in pull requests.
relevance: Static counterpart to APIClarity: infer the integration surface from source code rather than from live traffic, which needs repo access but no production tap.
limitations: Not fetched. Open-core commercial vendor — the boundary between the free and paid tiers is exactly the thing that needs reading, not assuming. Security-tool framing means running it on a client estate carries its own authorization requirements.

claim: Captures real HTTP traffic from production or elsewhere and creates OpenAPI from it, for documentation, mocks, SDKs or contract testing.
relevance: Third variant of traffic-to-spec inference; more mature commercially than traffic2openapi.
limitations: Not fetched. Commercially backed with a paid cloud offering, so the open-source scope needs verification. Same payload-sensitivity concern as all traffic capture.

claim: Property-based API testing driven by OpenAPI and GraphQL schemas.
relevance: Downstream of discovery rather than part of it — validates a spec you already have.
limitations: Not fetched. Requires a schema as input, so it cannot discover anything; sends generated traffic at the target, which is unacceptable against a client's production system without explicit authorization.

claim: Exposes an operating system as a relational database, allowing SQL queries over installed applications, running processes, browser extensions and network connections.
relevance: Endpoint-side SaaS discovery: querying installed applications and browser extensions across a client's fleet reveals the real tool stack, including the shadow IT that never touched the IdP.
limitations: Not fetched. Requires agent deployment on employee machines — an IT-governance decision, not something an agency can arrange lightly. Named in the search results only as a composable building block, since no turnkey open-source shadow-SaaS discovery tool exists.

claim: Network security monitor generating structured logs of application traffic; can reveal SaaS usage by inspecting DNS queries, IP connections and TLS/SNI metadata without decrypting content.
relevance: The no-decryption route to shadow-SaaS discovery: DNS and TLS SNI alone reveal which cloud services a client's network talks to, which is a genuinely strong evidence source for 'what systems does this company actually use'.
limitations: Not fetched. Requires network tap placement inside the client's environment — heavy deployment and a serious authority boundary. Produces raw network telemetry about identifiable employees. Cited in search results as a composable ingredient, not a discovery product.

claim: Modular active-learning framework on scikit-learn: ActiveLearner with pluggable query strategies (uncertainty, entropy, custom), Committee/CommitteeRegressor for query-by-committee, BayesianOptimizer, ranked batch-mode sampling and information density; Keras integration.
activity: 2.4k stars, 325 forks, 739 commits; 94 open issues and 14 open PRs; CI badges still point at travis-ci.org, retired for open source years ago; last paper 2018
relevance: The direct formal answer to 'which question is worth asking next'. Model the unknowns about a client as a label space, treat each question as a label request, and let uncertainty sampling or query-by-committee rank candidate questions by expected information gain — so precomputed evidence removes questions from the queue automatically rather than by hand-written rules.
limitations: Maintenance is the concern: a dead-CI badge, a 94-issue backlog and a 2018 citation together read as low-activity rather than merely stable. The bigger gap is conceptual — these strategies rank items by classifier uncertainty, which is not the same as ranking questions by value to a human client; cost, intrusiveness and answerability are not modelled at all. Adopt the framing, expect to write the scoring function.

claim: Comprehensive active-learning library on scikit-learn implementing 60+ query strategies drawn from 40+ research papers, spanning pool-based and stream-based settings, with deep active learning via skorch/PyTorch.
activity: 201 stars, 24 forks, 2,531 commits; most recent citable work is a July 2025 preprint; Releases section appeared empty in the fetched page
relevance: The better-maintained and better-licensed sibling of modAL for question-selection policy. Its stream-based strategies matter more than the pool-based ones for Actionist: a client conversation is a stream where each potential question arrives and must be asked-or-skipped immediately under a budget, which is exactly the stream-based active-learning formulation with a labelling budget.
limitations: Its own README describes it as a library for research; expect research ergonomics rather than a production policy engine. Strategy count varies by source (search said 47 pool + 14 stream, the repo says 60+) — quote the repo's 60+ or, better, count the strategy overview page before quoting anything. 201 stars is a small community for a library carrying this much surface area. Same conceptual gap as modAL: uncertainty is a proxy for question value, not a measure of it.

claim: Optimal Bayesian Experimental Design for choosing measurement settings when a parametric model is known; selects settings likely to make parameter estimates more precise, aimed at cases where measurements are expensive.
license_claimed: not observed (NIST work is typically US public domain)
relevance: The theoretically correct frame for the question-selection problem: each question is an experiment with a cost, and you choose the one maximizing expected information gain about the client model. 'Measurements are expensive' is precisely why you precompute before asking — a client's attention is the scarce resource.
limitations: Not fetched. Requires a known parametric model of the system being measured, which a client organization emphatically is not; adopting this means adopting the maths, not the code. Physics-instrumentation oriented. NIST software is usually public domain rather than carrying a standard OSS licence, which has its own downstream implications.

claim: Framework for experimental design and multi-objective Bayesian optimization, built on Meta's BoTorch.
relevance: Multi-objective is the relevant part: choosing what to ask a client trades information gain against time cost and intrusiveness simultaneously, which is a constrained multi-objective problem rather than a single-score ranking.
limitations: Not fetched. Built for chemical/industrial process optimization over continuous parameter spaces; a question queue is discrete and combinatorial, so the fit is by analogy only. BoTorch/PyTorch is a heavy dependency for a scoring policy.

claim: General-purpose toolbox for Bayesian Design of Experiments focused on real-world experimental campaigns; claimed use in industry and academia.
relevance: Same borrowed frame as bofire; its explicit focus on real-world campaigns with human-in-the-loop constraints is closer to the messy client setting than pure BO libraries.
limitations: Not fetched. Corporate-backed (Merck KGaA) chemistry tooling; domain distance from client questioning is large. Maturity and licence unverified.

claim: Experimental design and Bayesian optimization library in Python/PyTorch.
relevance: Marginal — a third BO library in the same academic cluster.
limitations: Not fetched. Chemical-engineering research group tooling; no distinctive capability over bofire or BayBE for this use case.

claim: Toolbox for Bayesian Nonparametric Quasi-Experimental Design in Python.
relevance: Quasi-experimental design is about inferring effects without a controlled trial — conceptually relevant to judging whether an intervention helped a client when you cannot randomize, but not to question selection.
limitations: Not fetched. Single-academic research code; off the main thread of question-selection policy.

claim: Amortized Bayesian inference library; ships a Bayesian Experimental Design example notebook framing BED as combining information theory and Bayesian modelling to plan experiments maximizing information gain.
relevance: Amortization is the genuinely interesting idea for Actionist: train once so that at conversation time selecting the next question is a fast forward pass rather than an expensive per-client optimization.
limitations: Not fetched. BED is one example notebook, not the library's purpose. Amortized inference needs a simulator of the domain to train against, which for client organizations does not exist.

claim: Modular graph-based RAG system; an LLM-driven pipeline that extracts structured entities and relationships from unstructured narrative text and builds knowledge-graph memory structures used as targeted context for question answering.
activity: 35.7k stars, 3.8k forks, 491 commits. MAINTENANCE MODE: README states the project will not accept new PRs or implement new features; bug fixes and CVE-driven dependency updates only. 33 open PRs against 3 open issues
relevance: The pattern for turning a client's own documents — SOPs, contracts, onboarding decks, email threads — into a queryable organizational graph, so that questions already answered somewhere in their material are never asked. Its community-detection summarization is what enables answering global questions about a corpus rather than only retrieving passages.
limitations: Maintenance mode is decisive for a client deliverable: MIT-licensed and hugely popular, but feature-frozen by its own maintainers, and the 33-to-3 PR-to-issue ratio is a graveyard of unmergeable contributions. README warns indexing is expensive and advises starting small — per-client indexing cost is a real line item. Explicitly a research demonstration, not a supported Microsoft product. Out-of-the-box extraction quality is acknowledged as suboptimal without prompt tuning per domain.

claim: Framework for real-time temporal knowledge graphs for AI agents: incremental ingestion without full recomputation, bi-temporal fact validity windows with automatic invalidation on contradiction, provenance via 'episodes' linking every fact to its source, hybrid semantic + BM25 + graph-traversal retrieval, custom ontology through Pydantic entity and edge types.
activity: 30.3k stars, 3.1k forks, 952 commits; 285 open issues and 206 open PRs — heavily active. Underpins Zep's commercial context infrastructure
relevance: The best-fitting org-graph primitive found, for two reasons specific to client intelligence. Bi-temporal invalidation means when a client's situation changes the old fact is superseded rather than deleted, so the system knows what it used to believe and when that stopped being true. Episode provenance means every precomputed claim traces to the source document or conversation that produced it — the same defensibility property that makes fire-enrich's per-field citations valuable, but built into the data model.
limitations: Open-core: it is the engine under Zep's paid product, so expect the roadmap to serve that. Needs a graph database — Neo4j 5.26, FalkorDB, or Amazon Neptune plus OpenSearch Serverless; the lightweight embedded option (Kuzu) is explicitly deprecated because upstream is unmaintained, so there is no cheap local backend. Requires an LLM API key per ingestion, so graph construction has a running per-client cost. A 206-open-PR backlog against 285 open issues signals a project moving faster than it is being reviewed.

claim: Open toolkit for knowledge-graph extraction and construction (EMNLP 2022): named entity recognition, relation extraction, attribute extraction, event extraction and relational triple extraction, across standard, few-shot, document-level and multimodal settings; DeepKE-LLM branch, OneKE multi-agent extraction framework, MCP service tools.
activity: 4.5k stars, 750 forks, 1,706 commits; dated updates run through July 2026 (CCF ODTC incentive program), with MCP service tools added June 2025 and OneKE open-sourced Dec 2024; maintainers commit to long-term maintenance
relevance: The only project here offering trained extraction models rather than prompt-an-LLM: attribute extraction and event extraction map directly onto pulling structured facts about a client's organization out of their documents. The few-shot and document-level settings matter because a single client will never provide enough labelled examples for supervised training. MCP tooling means an agent can call these lightweight extractors instead of paying for a large model on every document.
limitations: Chinese-NLP heritage runs deep — cnSchema, Chinese-Alpaca-2-13B, bilingual IEPile — so English-only performance on Western business documents needs its own evaluation rather than being assumed. MIT covers the toolkit, but the individual models it downloads carry their own licences (a LoRA on Chinese-Alpaca-2 inherits Llama-2 terms), which is exactly the kind of layered-licence trap that a repo-level MIT badge hides. Research toolkit ergonomics; DeepKE-LLM needs a completely separate environment.

claim: Takes unstructured text, uses any OpenAI-compatible LLM (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, LiteLLM, OpenAI) to extract subject-predicate-object triplets, standardizes entities across document chunks, infers relationships to connect disconnected subgraphs, and renders an interactive graph.
relevance: The minimal viable document-to-graph pipeline, and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint abstraction means it can run entirely against a local model — which for client documents is the difference between sending a client's contracts to a third party and not.
limitations: Not fetched: licence, stars and maintenance unverified. Free-form SPO triplets without a fixed ontology produce inconsistent predicates across runs, so the graph is hard to query reliably. Note aimaster-dev/knowledge-graph-construction appears to be a fork or mirror of this same project — a reminder that apparent breadth in this segment is partly duplication.

claim: Obsidian plugin building a lightweight knowledge graph from notes via LLM entity extraction over a fixed 10-type ontology (PERSON, ORGANIZATION, CONCEPT, PROJECT, TOOL, EVENT, PLACE, DOCUMENT, METHOD, TOPIC) with free-form relationship verbs; hybrid entity resolution resolving most entities by hash lookup and reserving embedding search and LLM calls for genuinely ambiguous cases.
relevance: Two directly stealable ideas. The fixed 10-type ontology is close to what an organizational model actually needs (people, orgs, projects, tools, methods) and constrains extraction enough to be queryable, unlike free-form triplets. The tiered entity resolution — cheap hash first, expensive LLM only for ambiguity — is the right cost architecture when graphing many client documents.
limitations: Not fetched. An Obsidian plugin, so it is a pattern to copy rather than a component to embed. Small personal project; licence and maintenance unknown.

claim: Pipeline extracting entities and relationships from PDF, TXT and DOCX into RDF graphs, combining SpaCy rule-based NER with LLM extraction, plus deduplication and merging; SPARQL-queryable.
relevance: The RDF/SPARQL choice is the notable part: a standards-based graph a client could take with them or plug into existing semantic tooling, rather than a proprietary schema. Multi-format document ingestion (PDF/DOCX) matches what clients actually send.
limitations: Not fetched. Appears to be an individual portfolio-scale project; licence, maintenance and quality all unverified. RDF/SPARQL is heavier machinery than most agent retrieval paths need.

claim: Creates knowledge graphs in GraphML, GEXF and HTML from a source entity's Wikipedia page, with customised prompts per entity type and cache support for iteratively growing a graph.
relevance: Only the caching-and-iterative-growth mechanic transfers — building a client graph should be resumable and incrementally extendable rather than a single batch run.
limitations: Not fetched. Wikipedia-seeded by design, which is useless for a private company: the entire premise is that the entity already has an encyclopedia article. Wrong input domain for client intelligence.

claim: Builds knowledge graphs via generative models through Ollama/Gemini/LM Studio, with structured triple extraction source-grounded via langextract, graph augmentation to bridge disconnected components, schema-constrained customizable domains, Cytoscape.js visualization and GraphML output.
relevance: Source grounding via langextract is the relevant feature — each extracted triple ties back to the span of text it came from, which is the provenance property that makes a precomputed client fact auditable rather than a model assertion.
limitations: Not fetched. Individual research-scale project; licence and maintenance unknown. 'Graph augmentation to bridge disconnected components' means inventing edges the source text did not state — directly hostile to an evidence standard where inferred must be distinguishable from observed.
